Well....

Honestly, I'd say that the presumption underlying your question springs from the same problem as the impetus for it.

That is to say - those who believe that their offense means that others don't have the right to say that which offends them are making the same mistake as you appear to be making when you ask if they have the right to be offended.

The better question, in both cases, is "does any individual have the right to stop them?"

Does the offended party have the right to stop other people from saying things? I say no.

Do others have the right to stop the offended party from choosing to be offended? Again, I say no.

Broadly, I just think that's a much more reasonable way to look at rights. I don't believe that people have rights to do this thing or that thing, but that, in some limited number of cases, other people have the right to attempt to stop them. The right of an individual to choose to do any particular thing should be presumed first, then only denied when others can make the case that it's justifiably denied. Rights should be seen to be the default position, and the denial of rights the exception.
I think you have the right to be offended by anything and everything. You don't have the right to try to take someone else's freedoms away because you were offended.
